title: From Kumasi to the World: The Girl Who Built a Billion-Dollar Idea

pages.text: Every Friday after school in Kumasi, fourteen-year-old Serwaa helped her Auntie Afia unload crates of fresh red tomatoes from farming towns in the Bono East and Ashanti regions. By Sunday afternoon, the fierce afternoon heat had softened nearly a third of the unsold crates into spoiled pulp. ‘All that hard work in the sun,’ Auntie Afia sighed, ‘and so much food and money is lost before Monday morning.’

pages.alt: Fourteen-year-old Serwaa and Auntie Afia inspect crates of tomatoes in a warm Kumasi market stall where several crates have spoiled in the heat.

pages.text: On Monday in the JHS science room, Serwaa asked Mr Ofori a question that would not leave her mind. ‘Why don’t market traders and smallholder farmers use cold rooms?’ Mr Ofori explained that conventional refrigerated rooms cost a fortune, needed constant grid electricity, and broke down when power fluctuated. ‘Great businesses do not start with a wish to get rich, Serwaa,’ he said. ‘They start by solving a painful problem that affects thousands of people.’

pages.alt: In a JHS science classroom, Serwaa raises her hand while Mr Ofori stands beside a chalkboard drawing of a farm-to-market supply chain.

pages.text: With her classmate Kojo, Serwaa built their first prototype, an early working model crafted to test an idea. They lined a wooden crate with local coconut-husk insulation, fitted a small twelve-volt cooling fan powered by a borrowed solar panel, and placed a dish of water and a thermometer inside. Everyone at the school science club clapped, until they checked the crates after forty-eight hours.

pages.alt: Serwaa and Kojo assemble a small wooden box lined with coconut fibre and connected to a small solar panel on a school workbench.

pages.text: The first prototype failed! Moisture condensed on the inside walls, soaked the coconut fibre, and made the tomatoes mouldy even faster. Kojo wanted to give up, but Serwaa opened her engineering notebook and wrote: Test 1 failed, humidity trapped inside. ‘Failure is not the end of an invention,’ she told Kojo. ‘It is data telling us what to fix next.’

pages.text: Years of study and experimentation followed. While studying mechanical engineering at university in Kumasi, Serwaa and Kojo tested thirteen versions of their cooler. They sealed the insulation in recycled aluminium panels, added a phase-change thermal battery that stored cold energy during sunny hours to keep produce cool all night, and included a simple sensor that alerted farmers on basic mobile phones if a door was left open.

pages.alt: Now university engineering students in their twenties, Serwaa and Kojo test a sleek metal-lined solar cold box in a workshop.

pages.text: Their first real pilot unit stood beside Auntie Afia’s stall and two neighbouring farm cooperatives. Instead of spoiling in two days, tomatoes, garden eggs and green peppers stayed crisp for two full weeks! Farmers paid a small daily fee of five cedis per crate, far less than the thirty cedis they used to lose when produce rotted. The unit paid for its own maintenance through real value.

pages.text: Soon, forty farming communities across Ghana asked for units, but Serwaa and Kojo had a new problem: building forty industrial solar cold rooms cost millions of cedis they did not have. To scale, growing a business so it can serve many more customers, they needed outside capital. They registered their company formally and prepared to meet investors.

pages.alt: Serwaa and Kojo study a map of Ghana dotted with pins while reviewing blueprints and cost spreadsheets in their small office.

pages.text: In Accra, they pitched to a climate-technology investment fund. The investors offered capital in exchange for equity, a share of ownership in the company. Before signing a single page, Serwaa and Kojo worked with a qualified Ghanaian corporate lawyer and an accountant. They made sure the agreement was fair, kept strong founder ownership, and committed every cedi of investment to building factories and farmer hubs.

pages.text: Scaling across West and East Africa was hard work. In their third year, a shipping delay held up solar compressors for two months, and the team had to redesign the cooling unit so seventy percent of its parts could be manufactured right in Ghana. By training local technicians in Tamale, Sunyani, Takoradi and Ho, they turned a supply crisis into hundreds of skilled Ghanaian engineering and maintenance jobs.

pages.text: Ten years after that first mouldy crate in JHS, international business news announced that Serwaa and Kojo’s company had reached a valuation of one billion cedis, and was expanding globally. Back at her old school in Kumasi, a JHS student gasped, ‘Sister Serwaa, do you have a billion cedis sitting in your bedroom?’ Serwaa laughed warmly and stepped to the chalkboard to explain the truth.

pages.alt: Serwaa laughs warmly in her old JHS classroom in Kumasi as curious students gather around her beside the chalkboard.

pages.text: ‘No!’ explained Serwaa. ‘A company’s valuation is not cash in a founder’s pocket. Our company is divided into ten million shares, and investors currently value each share at one hundred cedis, making ten million times one hundred equal one billion cedis on paper. Almost all that value lives in our factories, solar hubs, trucks and research labs. Even more importantly, billion-dollar companies are rare exceptions, never a guaranteed reward.’

pages.alt: Serwaa points to a visual diagram showing factories, solar cold rooms, delivery vans and workers rather than a pile of cash.

pages.text: ‘Whether a business grows to serve one neighbourhood in Kumasi or forty countries across the world,’ Serwaa told the students, ‘true success is measured by the problems you solve, the honest jobs you create, and the lives your work improves. Start by noticing a real need right where you are, learn your science and maths well, and never be afraid to build!’

activities.question: What happened to Serwaa and Kojo’s very first wooden prototype?
options: Trapped moisture condensed inside and made the tomatoes mouldy
It froze the tomatoes into solid ice overnight
Investors immediately bought it for a million cedis
activities.explanation: Their first prototype trapped humidity inside, soaking the coconut fibre, teaching them what to improve next.

activities.definition: A share of ownership in a company
distractors: A type of solar battery used in cold rooms
A fine paid when a prototype fails

activities.question: Why does a 1-billion-cedi company valuation NOT mean Serwaa has 1 billion cedis in cash?
options: Valuation is share price times total shares, tied up in company assets
The government takes ninety-nine percent of all company shares
Investors keep all the money locked in a glass box
activities.explanation: 10,000,000 shares × 100 cedis = 1,000,000,000 cedis in paper valuation, represented by factories, hubs and equipment rather than personal cash.

activities.prompt: Order the stages of Serwaa and Kojo’s entrepreneurial journey.
items: Observing tomato spoilage in Kumasi and testing early prototypes.
Refining the engineering design at university and running farm pilots.
Raising equity investment to build local factories and create jobs.

activities.prompt: How did Serwaa respond when Test 1 failed, and why does she value solving problems over chasing fame?

glossary.definition: An early working model built to test a design concept and learn what needs improvement
Material that slows the transfer of heat so a cool space stays cool longer
To grow a business system so it can serve many more customers reliably
Money or financial resources invested to build equipment, factories and operations
The estimated total economic worth of a company (total shares multiplied by share price), not cash in a founder’s pocket
